image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: Acquitted by the trial court
chapters.html: Judge Atma Charan acquitted Savarkar. The prosecution’s case did not establish his guilt; the acquittal was not overturned in the appeals involving the other defendants. [24, 26]

image.alt: Document · The Bombay Chronicle reports the trial verdict, 11 February 1949.
image.caption: Document · The Bombay Chronicle reports the trial verdict, 11 February 1949.
image.author: The Bombay Chronicle

chapters.title: Welcoming the Republic
chapters.html: In a message issued before Republic Day, he welcomed the inauguration of independent India’s republic and called for unity and national defence. [23]

image.alt: Historical context · Members of the Constituent Assembly take their pledge, 15 August 1947.
image.caption: Historical context · Members of the Constituent Assembly take their pledge, 15 August 1947.
image.author: Unknown author

chapters.title: Detention under independent India
chapters.html: He was detained during the period of the Nehru–Liaquat Pact. After release with political restrictions, he resigned even primary membership of the Hindu Mahasabha. [23]

image.alt: Undated historical portrait of V. D. Savarkar.
image.caption: Undated historical portrait of V. D. Savarkar.
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: Asking an old associate to write
chapters.html: His letters urged S. R. Rana to preserve memories of the revolutionary movement in Europe. The correspondence shows an active effort to shape the record future historians would inherit. [23]

image.alt: Historic site · 65 Cromwell Avenue, Highgate, his London residence, a modern view.
image.caption: Historic site · 65 Cromwell Avenue, Highgate, his London residence, a modern view.
image.author: Spudgun67

chapters.title: Closing Abhinav Bharat
chapters.html: At a public function, Savarkar announced the dissolution of the old revolutionary organisation. He presented the achievement of independence as the completion of its founding objective. [27]

image.alt: Family photograph · The Savarkar brothers with Shanta, Maina and Yamuna; before 1950.
image.caption: Family photograph · The Savarkar brothers with Shanta, Maina and Yamuna; before 1950.
image.author: Maharashtra state archives

chapters.title: Six Glorious Epochs
chapters.html: His final major historical work interpreted Indian history through resistance and the survival of Hindu political power. It extended themes of nationhood, warfare and historical memory developed in earlier books. [28]

image.alt: Undated historical portrait of V. D. Savarkar.

image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: The death of Yamuna
chapters.html: Yamuna Savarkar died in 1963. Her life had spanned the London years, long imprisonment, Ratnagiri restrictions and the family’s later residence in Bombay. [27]

image.alt: Family photograph · The Savarkar brothers with Shanta, Maina and Yamuna; before 1950.
image.caption: Family photograph · The Savarkar brothers with Shanta, Maina and Yamuna; before 1950.

chapters.title: His final illness and death
chapters.html: After prolonged ill health, Savarkar stopped accepting food and medicine in his final weeks. He died on 26 February 1966, aged eighty-two, describing his decision through the idea of atmarpan. [1, 32]

image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: The Kapur Commission’s record
chapters.html: The commission examined statements from secretary Gajanan Damle and bodyguard Appa Kasar concerning visits by Godse and Apte. Their accounts formed part of its reconstruction of the conspiracy. [25]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Accused in Gandhi’s assassination case; Savarkar is seated second from the left.
image.caption: Historical photograph · Accused in Gandhi’s assassination case; Savarkar is seated second from the left.
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: A finding different from the acquittal
chapters.html: The commission attributed the murder conspiracy to Savarkar and his group. It reported after his death and was an inquiry commission, not a criminal court conducting another trial. [25, 26]

image.alt: Historical photograph · Accused in Gandhi’s assassination case; Savarkar is seated second from the left.
image.caption: Historical photograph · Accused in Gandhi’s assassination case; Savarkar is seated second from the left.
image.author: Unknown photographer

chapters.title: The acquittal and the inquiry distinguished
chapters.html: The Supreme Court said the commission’s observations could not overturn his acquittal. It declined to reopen the case or decide the correctness of the commission’s findings. [26]

veer-savarkar.sourcesHtml:
1. Lok Sabha Secretariat, Swatantryaveer Vinayak Damodar Savarkar (2019). An official commemorative biography, used for birth, education and literary activity. Its praise is the institution’s assessment. Its stated age at death and some compressed chronology require checking against the actual dates. Official booklet.

  2. South Asian Britain: Connecting Histories, “Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.” A scholarly biographical resource for family, college, London associates and later restrictions. Claims about responsibility for particular weapons are not treated as established merely because they appear in a secondary biography. Biographical record.

  3. Government of Maharashtra, Source Material for a History of the Freedom Movement, volume II, “Swadeshi and Boycott.” Reproduces contemporary reports on the Pune procession, Savarkar’s appeal and the burning of foreign goods. These are colonial surveillance accounts, not neutral transcripts of every participant’s intentions. Document collection.

  4. English Heritage, “Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.” Used for the scholarship, India House address and London residence. The institutional record differs from the parliamentary account over his call to the Bar; this draft follows the latter’s explicit distinction between examinations and admission. Plaque and historical account.

  5. Chitragupta, Life of Barrister Savarkar (1926), childhood and imprisonment chapters. An early sympathetic biography, used as an attributed account of family bereavements and the brothers’ experiences. This manuscript does not settle disputed claims about the identity of its pseudonymous author. Digitised text.

  6. V. D. Savarkar, The Indian War of Independence, 1857 (1909), including the opening discussion of swadharma and swaraj. Savarkar’s interpretation and the later publisher’s notes are distinguished from the events of 1857 themselves. Text and publisher’s note.

  7. V. D. Savarkar, News Letters from London, with the edition’s introductory chronology. Used for the Mazzini publication and the consequences of the Pune boycott protest. The retrospective chronology is identified as editorial material, distinct from the dated letters. Collected text.

  8. Bombay High Court, Emperor v. Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, 6 October 1910, (1911) 13 Bom LR 296. A jurisdiction ruling, not the final sentencing judgment. Court’s historical report; searchable judicial text.

  9. *Permanent Court of Arbitration, Arrest and Return of Savarkar (France / Great Britain), award of 24 February 1911.* The tribunal addressed the arrest and return of the escaped prisoner, not whether he was guilty of the Indian criminal charges. Case and original award.

  10. Jean Longuet, submission in the Savarkar arbitration (1911). The submission records the two Indian prosecutions and sentences while arguing Savarkar’s side of the international custody dispute. The English version is Anurupa Cinar’s translation; its advocacy is not adopted as a finding of innocence. English translation.

  11. V. D. Savarkar, Majhi Janmathep (1927), English translation My Transportation for Life. A retrospective participant memoir: arrival and labour in the Andamans, prisoners’ organisation, transfer to mainland prisons and conditional release. The digitised translation uses its own page numbering. English text.

  12. V. D. Savarkar, “Oh Martyrs” (10 May 1908), and Letters from Andamans. The linked compilation begins with the London leaflet before the prison correspondence. These are political writings and censored letters, not an independent account of all prison events. Collected texts.

  13. Savarkar’s petitions of 14 November 1913, 1914 and 30 March 1920. The reproductions identify the National Archives of India as the source. Read the document images and the petitions’ actual requests separately from the modern publisher’s polemical framing. The 1913 petition itself refers to an earlier application in 1911. Petitions and reproduced records.

  14. M. K. Gandhi, letter to N. D. Savarkar, 25 January 1920, Collected Works, document 277. The addressee was Narayan, not Vinayak. The dated letter concerns a 1920 release campaign and does not establish that Gandhi advised the earlier petitions. Letter reproduced by Gandhipedia.

  15. M. K. Gandhi, “Savarkar Brothers,” Young India, 26 May 1920; Collected Works, document 139, printed pp. 368–370 in the linked volume. A public argument about the amnesty and the brothers’ continued custody. Digitised Collected Works volume.

  16. V. D. Savarkar, Essentials of Hindutva (1923). His own definition of Hindu identity, its distinction from Hinduism, and its territorial, ancestral and sacred-geographical conditions. The modern PDF’s introductory claim about completion in the Andamans conflicts with the author’s mainland custody dates; the draft places publication in 1923 without adopting that claim. Text; first-edition scan.

  17. Savarkar, writings on caste, translated extracts with references to Samagra Savarkar Vangmaya, volume III. Relevant citations include 1930–1931 essays, pp. 444–479; 1935 discussions, pp. 55–75; and the discussion of caste associations, pp. 620–624. Translated extracts and references.

  18. Savarkar, writings on the seven prohibitions, with named dates and collected-work references. Covers dining, caste exclusion, sea travel, ritual and reconversion; the treatment is his reform programme within Hindu consolidation. Translated extracts.

  19. District Ratnagiri, Government of Maharashtra, tourism account of Patit Pavan Mandir. The district page dates building activity to 1929; this should be distinguished from the temple’s opening in 1931. The draft avoids the unsupported claim that no earlier temple anywhere admitted excluded communities. District account.

  20. Savarkar memorial, accounts of Bhagojisheth Keer and other social-reform associates. Gives Keer’s role and the foundation ceremony of 10 March 1929; read alongside the 1931 opening listed in the chronology. Reconstructed conversations are commemorative narration rather than verbatim contemporary records. Associates and temple history.

  21. V. D. Savarkar, Hindu-Pad-Padashahi, 1925 edition. A historical work whose interpretation of Maratha power forms part of Savarkar’s political thought. Original-edition scan.

  22. V. D. Savarkar, Hindu Rashtra Darshan, collected presidential addresses, 1937–1942. In the linked digital edition: 1937 address, pp. 3–14; 1938 address, pp. 15–36; 1939–1941 addresses, pp. 37–104; 1942 address, especially pp. 108–115. These supply his views on nations, civic rights, European minorities, Hyderabad, military recruitment, Quit India and coalitions. Statements about communities are attributed to Savarkar, not treated as facts about those communities. Collected addresses.

  23. V. D. Savarkar, Historic Statements, items from 1944–1952. Includes the 1 August 1944 message favouring Mookerjee as president; statements against Partition; the January 1950 Republic message; March 1950 letters to S. R. Rana; and the July 1950 resignation following detention and restrictions. Dated statements.

  24. Special Court, Red Fort, Judge Atma Charan, judgment in the Gandhi murder case, 10 February 1949. Savarkar was acquitted. His result is distinct from the convictions of other defendants. Trial judgment scan, reproduced by Bar & Bench; High Court’s appellate judgment in its official archive.

  25. Justice J. L. Kapur, Report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Conspiracy to Murder Mahatma Gandhi (1969), volume II, chapter 25, especially paragraphs 25.92–25.106, culminating on printed p. 303. The report discusses Damle and Kasar’s statements and reaches its own conclusion about the conspiracy. This was a posthumous commission report, not a judgment overturning the acquittal. Full report scans.

  26. Supreme Court of India, Dr. Pankaj Kumudchandra Phadnis v. Union of India, 28 March 2018, especially paragraphs 6–8. The Court distinguished the commission’s observations from an enforceable criminal judgment and declined to reopen the matter or rule on the correctness or fairness of the report’s observations. Official judgment.

  27. Savarkar memorial, “Chronology of Savarkar’s Life.” Used for selected family and later-life dates and the Ratnagiri restrictions, with cross-checks against other records. This commemorative chronology contains inconsistencies: for example, it dates a Bose visit to June 1941 when he was already abroad, differs over the second sentence’s day, and states an age at death inconsistent with the birth and death dates. Those claims are not reproduced here. Chronology.

  28. V. D. Savarkar, Six Glorious Epochs of Indian History, English translation of his late Marathi work. Used to identify his historical method and continuing emphasis on Hindu political resistance, not as independent proof of every ancient or medieval episode it narrates. Text via the author’s collection.

  29. Central Information Commission, record concerning access to the Gandhi assassination files, especially the chronology of trial and appeals. An official later account of the case records rather than a new investigation into criminal guilt. Official decision and record summary.

  30. Government of India, Home Department proceedings, June 1921, proceeding no. 201. Contains material on the amnesty and the Savarkar brothers, including Yamunabai’s petition of 18 April 1921. The scan’s modern filename is not the original document title. Reproduced proceedings.

  31. Savarkar’s written statement in the Gandhi assassination trial (1948). A defence statement challenging the prosecution’s alleged conversations and the approver’s inference. Its denials are identified as his defence rather than an independent finding. Statement.

  32. V. D. Savarkar, “Suicide and Self-Sacrifice,” translated from his late essay. Used for his own explanation of the term atmarpan. Translated essay.
